Students will learn, from an engineer’s point of view, the theory and practice behind safely operating a 2-Axis CNC Turning Center. This course expands on the tooling geometry, speed, and capabilities covered in the manual turning class, ENG 199ML1, as well as part design, toolpath generation using CAD/CAM systems, machine navigation, and special tooling for CNC machines. Students will also turn several test parts within specified tolerances. This course is designed, in part, to help engineers understand manufacturability and processes involved in realizing their designs. Prerequisite: ENG 199 ML1, Intro to Turning for Engineers. Meeting dates will be arranged with instructor. Meets Monday from either 5:00 pm to 7:00 pm or 7:00 pm to 9:00 pm for 12 weeks, Course takes place in the Engineering Senior Design Lab.

Students will learn, from an engineer’s point of view, the theory and practice behind safely operating a manual lathe to produce precision parts. The curriculum covers the components of a manual lathe, their functions, and proper usage, and basic metrology. Students will develop the skills to select appropriate tooling, fixturing methods, spindle speeds, and feed rates for various applications and part metallurgy. Students will also turn a test part within specified tolerances. This course is designed, in part, to help engineers understand manufacturability and processes involved in realizing their designs. Times arranged with the instructor: select two days from M,Tu,W,Th,F at 12:15-2:45pm or 3:15 to 5:45pm for three weeks. This will be held in the Engineering Senior Design Lab.

Students will learn, from an engineer’s point of view, the theory and practice behind safely operating a TIG welder to create high strength joints in steel. The curriculum covers basic history of electro-arc welding as well as the properties of stick, MIG, and TIG welding. Students will develop the skills to prepare, create, and troubleshoot TIG welds in steel. Students will also weld a test joint to withstand mechanical force testing. This course is designed, in part, to help engineers understand manufacturability and processes involved in realizing their designs. Meeting dates are arranged with instructor. Class meets for two weeks. Week one has lecture Sunday from 6:00 pm to 10:30 pm, and hands-on instruction on either Tuesday or Thursday from 3:00 pm to 5:30 pm. Week two has a shorter lecture from 6:00 pm to 8:30 pm and identical hands-on instruction times. Course takes place in the Engineering Student Projects Lab.

sections.sectionText: Undergraduate Research in Scientific Advancement (URSA) is a research program that aims to provide first-hand research experience to underclassmen in STEM fields. The URSA program pairs graduate mentors up with undergraduate students on a semester-long research project and expects students to produce and present posters at the year-end symposium. Student must apply and be accepted to URSA before enrolling in this course. For further details, please visit: https://pure.engr.illinois.edu/.

Students will learn, from an engineer’s point of view, the theory and practice behind safely operating a waterjet system to manufacture parts from sheet material. The curriculum covers the basic methods to design and manufacture parts via waterjet, using integrated OMAX CAD/CAM programming systems, and others. Students will develop the skills to design within machine limitations, adjust machine parameters to improve produced parts, and use secondary finishing tools to refine waterjet-cut parts. Students will also cut a test part within specified tolerances. This course is designed, in part, to help engineers understand manufacturability and processes involved in realizing their designs. Meeting dates will be arranged with instructor on Tuesdays and Thursdays from 6:00 pm - 8:30 pm for two weeks. Course takes place in the Engineering Senior Design Lab.

Students examine the political developments that gave rise to apartheid and analyze the structure and consequences of the apartheid regime, particularly its impact on healthcare access and provision, technology, research, and development. sections.sectionText: This course emphasizes discussion, debate, and critical inquiry to demystify contemporary leadership paradigms. Students will explore leadership styles, characteristics, and practices relevant to student leaders through active dialogue and reflection. The course examines peer influence, role-modeling, and strategic approaches as essential frameworks for effective student leadership and peer mentoring. Learning experiences include selected readings, facilitated discussions, conversations with alumni, and reflective assignments that deepen understanding of leadership as a relational practice. Students interested in peer mentoring through the MEP Mentoring Course (ENG 111) are strongly encouraged to enroll.

With an interactive discussion/team-based approach, this course prepares students participating in international projects through Grainger Engineering RSOs for success at their project locations. Students will have the opportunity to critically reflect on both domestic and international experiences, develop their international travel plans, and participate in global engagement activities. Through their project destinations, students explore topics related to intercultural understanding, cultural values, and student engagement.

sections.sectionText: ENG 491 CU1 - Nanosatellite Design and Build 1 is an advanced course focusing on the in-depth tools and techniques used in spacecraft development. It covers topics such as link and power budgets, orbit analysis, and spacecraft testing with lab equipment like thermal vacuum chambers (TVAC), solar simulators, and center of gravity/moment of inertia measurement tools. Students engage heavily in CubeSat projects, applying advanced concepts to real satellite missions and testing. The course has a strong lab component, emphasizing independent project work and hands-on experience in spacecraft testing and mission development. Students should take AE 298 INS (Intro to Nanosatellite Design) prior to taking ENG 491 CU1.

sections.sectionText: This course will introduce the learner to the current risks and threats to an organization’s systems and data, combined with a structured way of addressing the safeguarding of these critical assets. The course also provides a foundation for those new to cybersecurity by delivering the broad-based knowledge and skills necessary to prepare students for further study in other specialized cybersecurity courses/fields. Course topics include threats, attacks, and vulnerabilities; Governance, Risk, and Compliance (GRC); Identity and Access Management (IdAM); physical security; cryptography and Public Key Infrastructure (PKI); security engineering; security operations; and security testing.
